Mark Formanek’s 24-hour performance video Standard Time captures 70 shift workers manually assembling and rearranging wooden planks to form a digital time display. Filmed at Berlin’s Sculpture Park, the workers in helmets and casual attire erect tall wooden frames on a concrete pad, set against a backdrop of apartment blocks and the iconic Berlin TV tower.

10.description:
William Kentridge’s 2012 installation The Refusal of Time occupies a dimly lit gallery, where a wooden mechanical sculpture stands at the center, flanked by steel megaphones and a breathing machine. Chairs are arranged around the piece, inviting viewers to sit and watch five-channel video projections on the walls. Silhouetted figures appear to manipulate clocks, engage in laboratory scenes, and enact vignettes of political resistance, all rendered through stop-motion animation and charcoal drawings.

12.description:
Visitors sit and recline on low sofas in a darkened gallery, their attention fixed on a large projection of two black-and-white clock faces. The installation, Christian Marclay’s The Clock (2010), runs continuously for 24 hours, stitching together thousands of film and television clips that feature clocks and references to time.

On view on the second floor of the Museum of Modern Art in New York until May 11, 2025, the work transforms the gallery into an immersive temporal experience. Member previews were held in the days before the public opening, inviting audiences to engage with the relentless passage of cinematic time.

13.description:
Tehching Hsieh, dressed in a pale grey worker uniform, stands before a wall-mounted time clock, inserting a yellow time card. Photographed by Michael Shen in New York in 1981, this image documents the artist’s commitment to punching the clock every hour on the hour for one full year. The minimalist setting—a plain wall and a simple clock—underscores the endurance and ritual at the heart of the performance.

Presented in the Living Time exhibition at the PHI Foundation’s DHC Session series in autumn 2009, this work exemplifies Hsieh’s radical melding of art and life. The photograph remains a powerful testament to the passage of time and the human relationship with routine and survival.

15.description:
John Cage’s 4'33" score abandons traditional notation in favor of vertical lines that map out four minutes and thirty-three seconds of silence. Created in 1952/1953, the ink-on-paper work visually represents the three movements’ durations through spatial intervals. 

Premiered by pianist David Tudor in Woodstock, New York, the piece transforms ambient noises—wind, rain, audience murmurs—into the performance itself. This unique score, acquired by MoMA through Henry Kravis’s generosity, exemplifies Cage’s exploration of chance and the redefinition of music.

16.description:
Jonathan Schipper’s installation stages a head-on collision between two full-sized automobiles, each advancing at roughly one millimeter per hour. The white and dark vehicles meet in a gallery space with exposed brick walls, their fenders and hoods gradually crumpling together. Over months, the imperceptible movement transforms a momentary crash into a prolonged meditation on desire, death, and entropy.

By stretching a violent event into a slow ritual, the work allows viewers to examine the deformation of metal and glass in detail. The decelerated collision becomes a three-dimensional time machine, inviting reflection on the fleeting nature of life and the spectacle of destruction.

17.description:
Dan Graham’s 1974 installation Present Continuous Past(s) transforms a simple gallery room into a temporal labyrinth. Live video cameras capture the space and its occupants, then project the images back onto the walls with a delay of a few seconds. The result is a continuous loop of real-time action and its recent past, overlaid on mirrored surfaces that multiply and fragment the viewer’s reflection.

Bruce Nauman’s 1970 installation presents a 30-foot-long, narrow white hallway formed by two parallel plywood and plaster walls. Visitors enter without instructions, feeling the walls brush against their shoulders and hips as they proceed toward two boxy television monitors stacked on the floor at the far end.

19.description:
Rafael Lozano-Hemmer’s Pulse Room installation transforms a darkened gallery into a living network of light and rhythm. Visitors place their fingers on a heart-rate sensor in the corner, and their pulses are transmitted to individual incandescent bulbs. Each bulb glows and flickers in time with a recorded heartbeat, then shifts across the grid as new participants join, creating an evolving constellation of human rhythms.

20.description:
Random International’s Rain Room at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art immerses visitors in a darkened chamber of perpetually falling water. Motion sensors detect each person’s presence, causing the rain to pause around them and allowing them to walk through the downpour without getting wet. The backlit silhouettes and reflective wet floor create dramatic shadows and a sense of wonder.

Presented from November 1, 2015, to January 22, 2017, as part of The Hyundai Project: Art + Technology, the installation was organized by LACMA and supported by Restoration Hardware and numerous patrons.
